```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Nonprofit mergers are rare, hard to see, and easy to confuse with other ways
an organization winds down. **npmerger** builds research datasets of
mergers from IRS Form 990 e-file data:

1. It finds candidate transactions in **Schedule N**.
2. It decides which of them are mergers rather than closures or asset sales.
3. It assembles the tables needed to study what happens to the organizations
   involved.

Data comes from the NCCS e-file release through
[panel990](https://nonprofit-open-data-collective.github.io/panel990/), and
fiscal-health metrics come from
[fiscal](https://github.com/Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/fiscal).

> **Status.** The full pipeline works, from Schedule N through the analysis
> tables. The classifier has been checked against 300 hand-labeled filings;
> see
> [How the classifier separates mergers from other cases](classifier.html)
> and the
> [roadmap](https://github.com/Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/npmerger/blob/main/PLAN.md).

## What counts as a merger

Following the Wilder Research study of Minnesota mergers, a merger is the
integration of two or more organizations into one legal entity, in which at
least one organization ceases to exist and its programs, assets, or staff
move to the successor. In 990 data that means three things have to be
visible:

* **The donor closes.** It files Schedule N Part I (liquidation,
  termination, or dissolution). Its final return usually shows assets
  near zero.
* **Its assets go to a nonprofit successor.** One nonprofit recipient
  receives most of the transferred value. Assets that are scattered across
  many charities, or go to individuals or businesses, look like a closure.
* **People go with them.** Officers, directors, or key employees join the
  successor.

The recipient keeps operating in almost every case, so that condition
adds little information. Leadership continuity and the concentration of
transferred assets are what separate a merger from a closure.

## Where the evidence comes from

**Schedule N.** Part I lists each asset distributed by an organization that
dissolved: a description, the date, fair market value (FMV), and the
recipient's name, EIN, address, and IRC section. Part II lists the same for
an organization that disposed of more than 25% of its net assets and kept
operating. Lines 2a–2c ask whether any officer, director, trustee, or key
employee became a director, employee, or owner of the successor.

**Part VII.** Those Schedule N boxes are under-reported. npmerger also
matches the people listed on the donor's Part VII (years t-1 and t)
against the recipient's Part VII (years t and t+1). In 2019–21 data, 87–100%
of donor–recipient pairs that checked a box shared at least one person,
against 9% for closures. About 40% of asset transfers with no box checked
shared people too. Leadership continuity counts when either source shows
it.

**Schedule N's own text.** When the asset descriptions or Part III
explanation say the transfer is part of a merger or consolidation
(`sn_merger_pattern()`), that counts as merger evidence on its own. In hand
validation every terminated filing with one successor and such text read as
a merger.

**Corroborating disclosures.** These are recorded for every filing. With
`merger_rules(promote = TRUE)`, a dissolution to one nonprofit successor
with no other merger evidence is promoted to a merger when at least two of
them agree. Promotion is off by default, because in hand validation few
promoted filings read as mergers. The signals are:

* merger language in the donor's Schedule O narrative;
* merger language in the recipient's Schedule O narrative;
* a significant change to the recipient's governing documents (Part VI
  line 4) in the merger year or the year after.

**Affiliation** is recorded separately from the label. It covers Schedule R
links, 509(a)(3) supporting organizations, group exemptions, and chapters.
About a third of two-party mergers and two-thirds of multi-party mergers
happen inside one family of organizations, and many analyses will want to
separate them from arm's-length mergers.

## Transaction types

```{r}
library(npmerger)
transaction_types()
```

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `merger2` | Dissolved; one dominant nonprofit successor; leadership continuity or corroboration |
| `mergerN` | The same, where the successor absorbs two or more dissolving organizations |
| `consolidation` | A `mergerN` into a newly formed entity |
| `asset_transfer` | Dissolved; one dominant nonprofit successor; no continuity evidence |
| `closure` | Dissolved; assets dispersed, or not going to a nonprofit |
| `asset_disposition` | Part II only: more than 25% of net assets transferred, organization continues |
| `reorganization` | Assets transferred to the filer's own EIN |

A first pass over 2019–21 filings (14,399 Schedule N returns) gave these
shares. This was before corroboration was applied, and it used Schedule N
flags or Part VII overlap as the leadership evidence:

| Label | Filings | Share |
|---|---|---|
| closure | 5,784 | 40% |
| asset_disposition | 3,250 | 23% |
| asset_transfer | 2,632 | 18% |
| merger2 | 2,306 | 16% |
| mergerN | 427 | 3% |

## The pipeline

`build_merger_data()` runs everything and returns every table:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
md <- build_merger_data(2019:2021, path = "PANEL990")
```

Each stage is also a separate function, so you can stop at any point,
inspect the result, or substitute your own step:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sn  <- get_schedule_n(2019:2021)   # Schedule N tables, via panel990
tx  <- sn_transactions(sn)         # one row per asset line, Parts I and II
tx  <- recover_recipient_ein(tx, get_name_index(2018:2022))  # fill missing EINs
fl  <- sn_filings(sn, tx)          # one row per Schedule N filing
ev  <- get_evidence_tables(fl)     # 990 tables for the donors and recipients
fe  <- merger_features(fl, ev)     # add the evidence to each filing
lab <- classify_transactions(fe)   # labels plus the evidence behind them
sched_n_table(lab)                 # YEAR, OBJECTID, EIN2, TYPE, evidence
```

`get_schedule_n()` downloads about 1 MB per tax year. `get_evidence_tables()`
is much heavier on its first run: Schedule O is about 150 MB per year and
Part VII about 100 MB. Both cache what they download, and the evidence step
then reads only the rows for the organizations involved.

`merger_features()` adds one group of columns per kind of evidence:

| Function | Adds | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `leader_overlap()` | `LEADER_P7`, `N_SHARED_P7` | Part VII names, donor t-1..t vs recipient t..t+1 |
| `add_donor_counts()` | `N_DONORS` | Other dissolving donors with the same dominant successor, t±1 |
| `add_filing_history()` | `FINAL_RETURN`, `DONOR_FILES_LATER`, `R_FORMED`, `R_NEW` | 990 header |
| `add_corroboration()` | `SO_MERGER_TEXT_DONOR`, `SO_MERGER_TEXT_RECIP`, `GOV_DOC_CHANGE_RECIP` | Schedule O, Part VI line 4 |
| `add_affiliation()` | `AFF_SCHED_R`, `AFF_SUPPORT_ORG`, `AFF_GROUP`, `AFFILIATED` | Schedule R Part II, Schedule A, group exemption number |
| `add_mission_similarity()` | `MISSION_SIM` | Part III mission statements |

### Cleaning

Schedule N is messy, and the low-level helpers handle the recurring
problems. Checkboxes come in several encodings:

```{r}
sn_flag(c("1", "true", "X", "0", "false", NA))
```

Recipient EINs arrive in many formats, including placeholders:

```{r}
clean_ein(c("01-0215911", "10215911", "000000000", "EIN-01-0215911"))
as_ein2("010215911")
```

The recipient's IRC section is free text, with dozens of spellings of
501(c)(3) alone:

```{r}
parse_irc_section(c("501(c)(3)", "501 C 3", "501(c)(6)", "LLC",
                    "Individual", "City of Portland", NA))
```

`sn_filings()` also deals with Schedule N's header and asset tables not
lining up. Some filings have only one or the other, so the filing list is
built from both.

### Classifying

`classify_transactions()` takes a filing-level table and adds a label, plus
the evidence used to reach it. Here is a small made-up example with one
filing of each kind:

```{r}
filings <- data.frame(
  case          = c("sale", "dispersed", "flags", "part7", "corroborated", "no evidence"),
  EIN2          = paste0("EIN-01-000000", 1:6),
  HAS_P1        = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE),
  HAS_P2        = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE),
  LEADER_SN     = c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE),
  LEADER_P7     = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
  N_NP_RECIP    = c(0L, 6L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L),
  TOP_SHARE     = c(NA, 0.2, 1, 1, 1, 1),
  TOP_RECIP_EIN = c(NA, "020000002", "020000002", "020000002", "020000002", "020000002"),
  SO_MERGER_TEXT_DONOR = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE),
  GOV_DOC_CHANGE_RECIP = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

out <- classify_transactions(filings)
out[, c("case", "LEADER", "N_CORROBORATE", "BASIS", "TYPE")]
```

The rules are arguments, so you can run strict and broad definitions side by
side. For example, a strict definition counts only the Schedule N boxes,
and a broad one turns promotion on:

```{r}
strict <- classify_transactions(filings, merger_rules(leader = "sn"))
broad  <- classify_transactions(filings, merger_rules(promote = TRUE))
data.frame(case = filings$case, strict = strict$TYPE, default = out$TYPE, broad = broad$TYPE)
```

`merger_rules()` also sets these thresholds and switches:

* the minimum share of transferred value going to the dominant recipient
  (`min_top_share`, default 0.75);
* whether a Part-II-only filing with the final-return box counts as a
  termination (`final_as_termination`, default `TRUE`);
* how many dissolving donors make a merger multi-party (`min_donors_n`);
* how recently a recipient must have been formed to count as a new
  entity (`new_entity_years`).

## Merger identifiers

Every donor–recipient pair gets an ID of the form `YEAR-FROMEIN-TOEIN`,
where the year is the donor's Schedule N tax year. A group ID ties together
all the donors that fold into one recipient:

```{r}
merger_id(2020, "01-0215911", "010431680")
merger_group_id(2020, "010431680")
```

## Output tables

The package ships a small extract of real 2021 filings, so the whole
pipeline can run offline. Here it is run without the **fiscal** ratios, to
keep this page quick:

```{r}
ex <- npmerger_example()
md <- build_merger_data(sn = ex$sn, evidence = ex$evidence, core = ex$core,
                        names = ex$names, bmf_data = ex$bmf,
                        ratios = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
md
```

### Schedule N table

`md$sched_n` has one row per Schedule N filing, with its label and the
evidence behind it:

```{r}
head(md$sched_n[, c("TAX_YEAR", "OBJECTID", "EIN2", "TYPE", "BASIS", "AFFILIATED", "N_DONORS")])
```

### Merger cases

`md$cases` has one row per donor–recipient pair.

* `MERGER_YEAR` is time 0 for the donor.
* `RECIP_MERGER_YEAR` is time 0 for the recipient: the recipient's tax year
  that contains the asset distribution date. It can differ from the
  donor's year when the two keep different fiscal years.
* `MERGER_GROUP_ID` and `N_GROUP` tie together the donors that fold into
  the same successor.

```{r}
md$cases[, c("MERGER_ID", "MERGER_GROUP_ID", "TYPE", "MERGER_YEAR", "RECIP_MERGER_YEAR", "N_GROUP", "FMV_TO_RECIP")]
```

### Value transferred

`md$transfers` breaks the reported fair market value down by asset class
(`asset_class()`).

* `FMV_ASSETS` excludes liabilities the recipient assumed.
* `COVERAGE` compares the transfer to the donor's beginning-of-year assets.
  Values far above 1 are flagged in `FLAG_OUTLIER`.

```{r}
head(md$transfers[, c("MERGER_ID", "FMV_TOTAL", "FMV_ASSETS", "FMV_CASH", "FMV_REAL_ESTATE", "COVERAGE", "FLAG_OUTLIER")])
```

### Donor and recipient attributes

`md$donors` and `md$recipients` share the merger ID and one layout:

* `SN_YEAR` and `REF_YEAR` (time 0 on that organization's calendar);
* name and address;
* formation and ruling years, and age;
* NTEE code;
* revenue, expenses, and assets for the five years up to `REF_YEAR`.

```{r}
d <- md$donors
d[1:3, c("MERGER_ID", "NAME", "STATE", "AGE", "NTEE", "REVENUE_TM4", "REVENUE_TM2", "REVENUE_T0", "ASSETS_T0")]
```

### Part VII panel

`md$part7` lists everyone on either organization's Part VII from t-2 to t+2.
`IN_BOTH` marks people who appear on both:

```{r}
p <- md$part7
p[IN_BOTH == TRUE][1:6, c("MERGER_ID", "ROLE", "TIME_FROM_MERGER", "PERSON_NAME", "TITLE", "COMP_ORG")]
```

### Fiscal panel

`md$fiscal` stacks the donor's years up to the merger and the recipient's
years before and after it, with harmonized 990 and 990-EZ measures.
Overhead, executive compensation, employees, and debt detail come from the
full Form 990 only.

```{r}
f <- md$fiscal
f[ROLE == "recipient"][1:6, c("MERGER_ID", "TIME_FROM_MERGER", "REVENUE", "EXPENSES", "ASSETS", "STAFF_EXP", "OVERHEAD_RATIO")]
```

With `ratios = TRUE` (the default), the panel also gets the ratios from
`fiscal::compute_all_panel()`. Two choices matter when you study change over
time:

* **A fixed calibration.** The ratios' winsorized and percentile variants
  are recomputed within each year. For an index that is comparable across
  years, fit `fiscal::fiscal_health_fit()` once on a reference sample and
  pass it (and `fiscal::fiscal_weights()`) as `fit` and `weights`.
* **Backward-looking smoothing.** `smooth = "trailing"` averages each
  organization's current and two previous years (`smooth_trailing()`).
  It never uses future years, so pre-merger values are not contaminated
  by post-merger ones. Use it for matching and baselines, and raw values
  for event-time outcomes.
